title: Integration By Parts
body:
**The product rule run backwards.** [[U-Substitution]] undoes the [[Chain Rule]]; this undoes the
product rule. Start from $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, integrate both sides, and rearrange:

$$
\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du
$$

It does not evaluate the integral. It **trades** it for a different one, and the whole skill is
choosing $u$ so the trade is a good one.

## Choosing $u$: LIATE

Pick $u$ to be whichever factor comes first in this list, and $dv$ is everything else:

| | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **L** | logarithmic | $\ln x$ |
| **I** | inverse trig | $\arctan x$ |
| **A** | algebraic | $x^2$ |
| **T** | trigonometric | $\sin x$ |
| **E** | exponential | $e^x$ |

The logic is that $u$ gets **differentiated** and $dv$ gets **integrated**, so $u$ should be the
thing that gets simpler when differentiated ($\ln x \to 1/x$ is a huge win) and $dv$ should be the
thing you can actually integrate. LIATE is a heuristic, not a theorem, but it is right almost every
time in a Calc 2 course.

## When it terminates

Parts is only useful if the new integral is easier. There are exactly two ways that pays off:

**1. The algebraic factor dies.** Each round drops the power by one, so $x^n$ needs $n$ rounds.

```
∫ x² eˣ dx      u = x²,  dv = eˣ dx
  = x²eˣ − ∫ 2x eˣ dx          (round 1)
  = x²eˣ − 2x eˣ + ∫ 2 eˣ dx   (round 2)
  = x²eˣ − 2x eˣ + 2eˣ + C     (round 3, plain integral)
```

**2. The original integral comes back and you solve for it.** Two rounds, then algebra.

```
I = ∫ eˣ sin x dx
  = −eˣ cos x + ∫ eˣ cos x dx
  = −eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x − ∫ eˣ sin x dx
  = −eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x − I

2I = eˣ(sin x − cos x)
 I = ½ eˣ(sin x − cos x) + C
```

The second one catches people out because after two rounds it looks like you have gone in a circle.
You have not: the circle is the answer. **Do not forget the $+C$ after dividing by 2.**

If neither happens and the new integral is worse, the choice of $u$ was wrong. Swap and retry.

## The one that looks like it has no product

$$
\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C
$$

Take $u = \ln x$ and $dv = dx$. There is nothing to pair $\ln x$ with, so pair it with $1$. Same
trick works for $\int \arctan x\,dx$ and $\int \arcsin x\,dx$, which is the whole reason **I** sits
so high in LIATE.

## Definite integrals

$$
\int_a^b u\,dv = \Big[uv\Big]_a^b - \int_a^b v\,du
$$

The $uv$ term gets evaluated at the limits immediately. Unlike [[U-Substitution]], the limits do
not change, because the variable never changed.

## Related

- [[Integration Techniques]] for when to reach for this rather than something else
- [[Chain Rule]] and [[Differentiation Rules]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] for the product rule this inverts
- [[Trigonometric Integrals]]: the reappearing-integral trick shows up there too, in the reduction
  formulas for $\int \sec^n\theta\,d\theta$
- [[Probability Density Function]] in [[STATISTICS]]: the expectation of an exponential
  distribution, $\int_0^\infty x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx$, is this technique plus an
  [[Improper Integral]]. So is every gamma-family integral
- [[Fourier Coefficients]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] are $\int f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx$, which
  is case 2 above whenever $f$ is trigonometric or exponential
